metadata.title: Multi-LLM Cooperation-Based Joint Intent-Driven Network Slicing and Resource Allocation
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes a multi-Large Language Model (LLM) cooperation-based Joint Network Slicing and Resource Allocation (JNSRA) algorithm to jointly optimize the configurations of intent-driven network slices and resource allocation in large-scale multi-BS networks. The JNSRA algorithm outperforms other Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and heuristic approaches, and the proposed multi-LLM collaboration can further enhance the reward, satisfaction ratio, and throughput.

sections.heading: Slicing and Resource Allocation
sections.text: Mingqi Han , Xinghua Sun , Member, IEEE , Huadong Li, Chenyuan Feng , Member, IEEE , Xijun Wang , Member, IEEE , Qiaofeng Xue, and Tony Q. S. Quek , Fellow, IEEE Abstract —The exponential growth of heterogeneous mobile applications has raised challenges in current Radio Access Networks (RAN). While the network slicing technique offers virtualized networks with independent resources to satisfy diverse Quality of Service (QoS) requirements, persistent chal- lenges remain in dynamic resource allocation and intent-driven slice configuration. For resource allocation, conventional Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based approaches encounter challenges in addressing the high-dimensional state-action space in large-scale networks with massive Base Stations (BS) and users. For slice configuration, current static intent-driven slice management frameworks suffer from inflexible architectures that fail to adaptively optimize network slicing configurations. In this letter, we propose a multi-Large Language Model (LLM) cooperation-based Joint Network Slicing and Resource Allocation (JNSRA) algorithm to jointly optimize the configurations of intent-driven network slices and resource allocation in large- scale multi-BS networks. In JNSRA, we propose to train Agent LLM through LLM alignment, which can enhance cooperation among slices and BS by regarding joint resource allocation actions as sequences. Moreover, we propose a multi-LLM joint optimization framework to jointly optimize Agent, leading to enhanced network slicing and resource allocation. Simulation results illustrate that JNSRA outperforms other DRL and heuris- tic approaches, and the proposed multi-LLM collaboration can further enhance the reward, satisfaction ratio and throughput. Index Terms —Radio access network, network slicing, large language model, resource rationing, multi-LLM cooperation. Received 29 August 2025; revised 11 December 2025; accepted 12 January 2026. Date of publication 20 January 2026; date of current version 2 February 2026. The diverse Quality of Service (QoS) requirements among users lead to a severe challenge for the next-generation Radio Access Network (RAN). To address this, wireless network slicing has been proposed [1] . sections.text: I NTEREST In this letter, we consider a downlink RAN slicing sce- nario as presented in Fig. 1 . The network comprises multiple coexisting BS, each of which serves different wireless users with distinct intents. The set of BS is denoted as K , and the set of users associated with BS k is denoted as N k . Each wireless user can be associated with at most one BS simultaneously. A. System Model Through centralized orchestration by the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC), the network is partitioned into multiple iso- lated slices, each dynamically allocated to serve specific user groups with diverse intent requirements. The set of network slices is denoted as M . Each BS k has independent bandwidth B k . In particular, we consider that adjacent BS operate with distinct bandwidths, which avoids inter-BS interference. At the beginning of the network, the RIC first generates slice configurations of each slice m ∈M for all BS. The state s m of slice m is characterized as s m = { d m , B min m , B max m } , (1) in which d m is the delay constraint of slice m and B min m denotes the minimum reserved bandwidth required by slice m for all BS [10] . B max m is utilized to limit the maximum bandwidth that can be allocated to each user, which can avoid excessive consumption on bandwidth resources by a few users and ensure fairness among users. After generating slice configurations, each BS k allocates its available bandwidth to each slice m ∈M . The total bandwidth of slice m in BS k is denoted as B k m . Similar to [2] , [3] , we consider that Orthogonal Frequency-division Multiple Access (OFDMA) is employed to avoid interference among users. Specifically, the slice bandwidth B k m of BS k is further allocated to each user n ∈N k within slice m . sections.heading: III. JNSRA A
sections.text: LGORITHM In this letter, we propose the multi-LLM cooperation- based JNSRA to jointly optimize the intent-driven network slicing and resource allocation. Towards this end, we propose to address this joint optimization problem in a multi-LLM collaborative manner [11] . In the following, we first illustrate Intent LLM that addresses the intent-driven network slicing problem and Agent LLM that addresses the large-scale joint resource allocation problem, and then demonstrate the multi- LLM collaborative training framework. A. Intent LLM In JNSRA, we implement DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B as Intent LLM, which processes natural language user intents and gen- erates formatted network slice configurations. The framework of network slice generation is illustrated in Fig. 2 . The natural language user intent is first inserted in the instruction prompt, which is then passed to Intent LLM to generate formatted responses. According to the given format, we can directly extract the network slice configurations a s . To ensure Intent LLM can generate formatted responses, we first pre-train Intent LLM in a Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) manner. As presented in the left part of Fig. 3 , we employ the original DeepSeek-R1 model as a teacher LLM to produce formatted responses and prompts for training data generation. This enables the intent model to learn proper response for- matting, which can then directly extract the network slice configurations a s . Denoting user’s intent prompt in Fig. 2 as p and the response as y , the SFT loss L SFT is given by L SFT = − 1 L L � t =1 log P ( y t | p , y < t , θ ) , (6) Fig. 2. Through (6) , Intent LLM maximizes the probability of the formatted response, which learns to provide the network slices in the given format. B. Agent LLM For the resource allocation, we adopt a Llama-based model with a cross-attention module as Agent LLM. As illustrated in the right part of Fig. 3 , Agent LLM takes slice information and network status as input state, and outputs the bandwidth resource allocation for all BS. Then, the corresponding envi- ronment reward r env is utilized to train Agent LLM in a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) manner [12] . In the following, we first illustrate the input state s , and then the environment reward r env . As aforementioned, the network state s n ∈ R K × 5 includes the status of all BS in the network, while the slice state a s ∈ R M × 3 includes the requirements of all slices, which can be regarded as different modals. Since the popular self-attention aims at processing inputs same modal, we deploy the cross- attention module to address it. We introduce the network slice state a s and the network state s n = { s k n } k ∈K separately. The network state s k n of each BS k is given by s k n = {|N k | , R k , B k , pos k } , (7) in which |N k | is the total number of users associated with BS k , R k represents its coverage area and pos k denotes its geometric position. In Agent LLM, the network slice state a s and the network state s n are processed through two different Llama-based models separately. Then, their hidden states are passed to the cross-attention module to jointly capture the correlations among BS and slices, which is then utilized to obtain the resource allocation action a B . sections.heading: ESULTS AND
sections.text: D ISCUSSIONS In this section, we evaluate the proposed JNSRA algorithm against several baselines. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce a centralized DDPG (c-DDPG) as the baseline of DRL, in which a transformer is adopted to capture correlations across BS and slices for optimization. Besides, we introduce three heuristic schemes as baselines, includ- ing Average, Weighted and Random. The Average equally allocates bandwidth resources for each slice, the Weighted allocates bandwidth resources according to the relative num- bers of users between slices, and the Random randomly allocates bandwidth resource a B . In the following, we con- sider a standard Urban Macro multi-cell setting, in which the network area spans 2km × 2km . The detailed network parameters are summarized in Table I . For network slicing, we introduce four typical network slices, including enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications (URLLC), voice, and massive Machine-Type Communications (mMTC). The transmission power P k is set to typical high-power macro cell transmission levels. For the bandwidth and other slice configurations, we adopt settings consistent with established simulation-based network slicing testbeds, including Slicesim [14] and Open5gs [15] . A. The performance comparison is presented in Fig. 4 a. Compared with others, JNSRA illustrates significantly better performance in terms of reward, satisfaction ratio and network throughput. Compared to c- DDPG, the performance improvement of JNSRA highlights that conventional DRL methods struggle with the high-dimensional state-action space since the actor’s update relies heavily on the critic’s Q-value gradients, which become unstable in such large combinatorial spaces. In contrast, the DPO-based Agent LLM avoids value-estimation errors and achieves substantial performance gains through sentence-level preference alignment. B. Joint Network Slicing and Resource Rationing Moving forward, we evaluate the performance of the proposed JNSRA in jointly optimizing network slicing and resource allocation. As Fig. 4 b illustrates, though both of them can generate appropriate responses to extract network slice configurations, the proposed JNSRA can improve the overall network performance compared to that with- out joint optimization, especially for the total reward. Specifically, JNSRA generates more strict delay requirements d m for eMBB and URLLC compared to that without joint optimization, thereby enhancing the QoS. For the voice and mMTC, JNSRA relaxes the delay requirements to accommo- date more users. Moreover, JNSRA optimizes the bandwidth allocation for mMTC by increasing the reserved bandwidth while reducing the maximum allocated bandwidth, which further improves the satisfaction ratio for mMTC users. These results highlight how joint optimization dynamically fine- tunes network slicing configurations to improve overall system performance. V. C

sections.heading: ONCLUSION AND
sections.text: F UTURE W ORK In this letter, we propose the LLM-enabled JNSRA algo- rithm to jointly optimize the network slicing and resource allocation strategy. In JNSRA, two independent LLMs are introduced, including Intent LLM that translates natural lan- guage intents into slice configurations and Agent LLM that addresses the high-dimensional state-action space of resource allocation. Moreover, we formulate the relationship of Intent LLM and Agent LLM using MDP, and propose a corre- sponding multi-LLM joint optimization framework, in which Intent LLM and Agent LLM can collaboratively improve the network slicing and resource allocation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed JNSRA achieves significantly better performance than conventional DRL and heuristic meth- ods, and the multi-LLM joint optimization can further enhance the network performance in terms of reward, satisfaction ratio and throughput.
